G4. Neighbours and borders
Problem 766. Crossing the fictional border network of Quartz
Knowledge context.
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.
Given facts.
Countries are represented by the fictional states Quartz, Grove, Harbor, Juniper, Fern, Linden. Shared borders: Quartz–Grove, Grove–Harbor, Harbor–Juniper, Quartz–Fern, Fern–Linden, Linden–Juniper.
Rules.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
Task.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Quartz to Juniper? Is Grove necessarily crossed?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Quartz to Juniper. 3. Remove Grove and check whether Juniper is still reachable from Quartz. 4. It is still reachable, so Grove is not unavoidable.
Answer.
3 border crossing(s); Grove is not unavoidable.
Knowledge takeaway.
Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.
Formal model.
Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.
